title: Observability and Monitoring Architecture
objectives: Design observability into systems from the start
Implement the three pillars of observability: logs, metrics, and traces
Design alerting that is actionable rather than noisy
Use observability to support incident response and continuous improvement
Meet GovAssure and Service Standard operational readiness requirements
whyThisMatters:
A service without observability is a service you cannot operate. When something goes wrong — and it will — you need to understand what happened, why it happened, and what the impact was. Without structured observability, incident response becomes guesswork: engineers stare at logs hoping to spot something, users report symptoms that cannot be correlated with causes, and the same failures recur because nobody understands the underlying pattern.

The UK Government Service Standard (point 14: operate a reliable service) requires that services can be monitored and supported effectively. GovAssure — the government's cyber security assessment framework — expects organisations to demonstrate they can detect and respond to operational and security incidents. These are not bureaucratic requirements; they reflect hard-won lessons from services that failed silently for hours before anyone noticed.

For architects, observability is not an afterthought bolted on before go-live. It is a fundamental design concern that shapes how services are built, how they communicate, and how they expose their internal state. The decisions you make about correlation IDs, structured logging, metric instrumentation, and trace propagation determine whether your future self — or the on-call engineer at 3am — can diagnose a problem in minutes rather than days.

content.heading: The Three Pillars of Observability
content.body:
Observability rests on three complementary data types, each providing a different lens on system behaviour.

Logs are discrete events — timestamped records of something that happened. A user logged in. A payment was processed. An error occurred. Structured logs (JSON format with consistent fields) are dramatically more useful than unstructured text because they can be queried, filtered, and correlated programmatically. Every log entry in a government service should include: a timestamp in ISO 8601 format, a correlation ID that traces the request across services, a severity level (DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR), the service name and version, and structured context relevant to the event.

Metrics are numerical measurements over time — counters, gauges, and histograms that reveal trends, patterns, and anomalies. Key metrics for government services include: request rate (how many requests per second), error rate (what percentage are failing), latency distribution (p50, p95, p99 response times), queue depth (how much work is waiting), and resource utilisation (CPU, memory, connections). The RED method (Rate, Errors, Duration) provides a minimum viable set for any service endpoint. The USE method (Utilisation, Saturation, Errors) covers infrastructure resources.

Traces follow a single request as it flows through multiple services, recording the timing and outcome of each step. In a distributed government service, a citizen's grant application might touch an API gateway, an authentication service, a business rules engine, a fraud check service, and a payment service. Without distributed tracing, when this request takes 8 seconds instead of 2, you cannot identify which service introduced the delay. Traces make the invisible visible.

The three pillars are complementary. Metrics tell you something is wrong (error rate spiked). Traces tell you where it is wrong (the fraud check service is timing out). Logs tell you why it is wrong (the fraud check's database connection pool is exhausted because a query is running without a timeout).

content.heading: Designing Observability In From the Start
content.body:
Observability should be a first-class architectural concern, designed in during alpha, not retrofitted before go-live. Retrofitting observability is expensive and incomplete — you end up with inconsistent logging formats, missing correlation IDs, and gaps in metric coverage that only reveal themselves during incidents.

Correlation IDs are the foundation of cross-service observability. Every request entering your system should receive a unique identifier (typically a UUID) that propagates through every service the request touches. This means: API gateways generate correlation IDs for incoming requests, services pass correlation IDs in HTTP headers (commonly X-Correlation-ID or traceparent in W3C Trace Context format), message queues include correlation IDs in message metadata, and every log entry includes the correlation ID. When an incident occurs, you can search for a single correlation ID and see the complete journey of a request across all services.

Structured logging standards should be defined at the architecture level, not left to individual teams. Agree on: the log format (JSON is the de facto standard), required fields (timestamp, correlation ID, service name, severity, message), sensitive data handling (never log PII, tokens, or credentials — use redaction patterns), and log levels (what constitutes ERROR vs WARN vs INFO). The GDS Way provides guidance on logging that aligns with these principles.

Metric instrumentation should follow the four golden signals identified by Google SRE: latency (how long requests take), traffic (how much demand the system is handling), errors (how many requests fail), and saturation (how full your resources are). Instrument these at every service boundary. Use histograms rather than averages for latency — averages hide outliers that matter to users.

Health endpoints expose a service's own assessment of its health. Implement both liveness checks (is the process running?) and readiness checks (can the service handle requests — are its dependencies available?). Kubernetes and most container orchestrators use these to make routing and restart decisions. A service that is live but not ready should not receive traffic.

content.heading: SLO-Based Alerting and Avoiding Alert Fatigue
content.body:
Alert fatigue is one of the most common operational failures in government services. Teams receive hundreds of alerts per day, most of which are false positives or require no action. Engineers learn to ignore alerts, and when a genuine incident occurs, it is lost in the noise.

Service Level Objectives (SLOs) provide a principled approach to alerting. An SLO defines the level of service you commit to providing — for example, '99.9% of requests complete successfully within 2 seconds.' Alerts fire when the error budget (the allowed 0.1% failure) is being consumed faster than expected, indicating a genuine risk to the service level.

Designing SLO-based alerting:

First, define SLOs that reflect user experience. 'CPU below 80%' is not an SLO — it is a resource metric that may or may not affect users. 'Citizens can submit applications within 3 seconds, 99.5% of the time' is an SLO because it describes what matters to users. For government services, consider SLOs around: availability (the service responds to requests), latency (responses arrive within acceptable time), correctness (responses are accurate), and freshness (data is up to date).

Second, calculate error budgets. If your SLO is 99.9% availability over 30 days, your error budget is 43 minutes of downtime per month. Alert when the burn rate suggests you will exhaust this budget — not on every individual error.

Third, create multi-window alerting. A short window (5 minutes) with a high burn rate catches acute incidents. A longer window (6 hours) with a moderate burn rate catches slow degradation. This avoids alerting on brief spikes that self-resolve while still catching persistent problems.

Fourth, every alert must be actionable. If an engineer receives an alert and their response is 'I do not know what to do about this,' the alert should not exist. Each alert should link to a runbook that describes: what the alert means, what to check first, common causes, and remediation steps. The Service Standard expects services to have documented support processes — runbooks are part of this.

Government-specific consideration: SLOs should align with the service levels published in your service's operational documentation. If your service dashboard promises '99.9% availability' to your programme board, your alerting should detect when that target is at risk — not after it has already been missed.

content.heading: Observability for Different Audiences
content.body:
Different stakeholders need different views of the same underlying data. A single dashboard that tries to serve everyone serves no one.

Operations team dashboards focus on real-time system health. They answer: is anything broken right now? What is the current error rate? Are any dependencies degraded? Which alerts are firing? These dashboards update every few seconds, show current state prominently, and are designed to be glanced at and understood immediately. They typically display the four golden signals for each service, dependency health status, and active incident count.

Service owner dashboards focus on trends and service level compliance. They answer: are we meeting our SLOs? How much error budget remains? What is the trend in response times over the past month? Where are the reliability risks? These dashboards update hourly or daily, show trends over weeks and months, and help prioritise reliability work. They are what you show at sprint reviews and service assessments.

Programme board dashboards focus on outcomes and risk. They answer: is the service reliable enough to meet user needs? What are the key operational risks? How does our reliability compare to our targets? These dashboards are deliberately simple — red/amber/green status, SLO compliance percentages, and trend arrows. Senior stakeholders do not need histograms; they need confidence that the service is well-managed and early warning when it is not.

Government performance dashboards (public-facing) show citizens and other departments how the service is performing. The Service Standard expects services to publish performance data. This might include: availability percentage, average transaction time, user satisfaction scores, and completion rates. These are typically sourced from the same observability data but aggregated and presented differently.

Design principle: instrument once, visualise many times. The underlying data (logs, metrics, traces) is the same. Different dashboards query and present it differently for different audiences. Do not build separate instrumentation for each audience — build rich instrumentation and create appropriate views.

content.heading: Observability in Incident Response and Continuous Improvement
content.body:
Observability earns its value during incidents. The difference between a 10-minute resolution and a 10-hour resolution is often the quality of observability data available to the responding engineer.

During incidents, observability should support: detection (automated alerting identifies the problem before users report it), triage (dashboards immediately show the scope and severity — how many users are affected, which services are involved), diagnosis (traces and logs pinpoint the root cause — not just which service failed, but why), and communication (real-time data supports incident communication — 'we have identified the issue, it affects 15% of users, and we expect resolution within 30 minutes').

Post-incident, observability supports blameless retrospectives. With good observability data, you can reconstruct the incident timeline precisely: what happened, when it happened, what signals were available, and what was missed. This moves retrospectives from 'who did what wrong' to 'what did our systems tell us, and how could we have detected this faster?'

Continuous improvement uses observability to identify reliability trends. Are error rates increasing slowly over time (suggesting accumulating technical debt)? Are certain endpoints consistently slower than others (suggesting optimisation opportunities)? Do incidents cluster around specific deployment windows (suggesting deployment process improvements)?

GovAssure expectations: the government's cyber security assessment framework expects organisations to demonstrate operational monitoring capabilities including: detection of anomalous behaviour, logging of security-relevant events, retention of logs for investigation purposes, and the ability to respond to incidents within defined timeframes. Your observability architecture must address these requirements.

The Service Standard assessment at beta and live examines whether the team can demonstrate: how they monitor the service in production, how they detect and respond to problems, what their incident management process is, and how they learn from incidents. A service without observability will not pass a live assessment.

Runbooks are the bridge between observability and action. For each alert, a runbook should document: the meaning of the alert, immediate diagnostic steps, common root causes and their remediation, escalation criteria (when to wake someone up vs when to wait for business hours), and communication templates for stakeholder updates. Runbooks turn observability data into operational confidence.

workedExample.title: Implementing Observability for a DESNZ Energy Grants Service
workedExample.context: DESNZ is preparing a new energy efficiency grants service for beta assessment. The service comprises: a citizen-facing application frontend, a caseworker assessment tool, an eligibility rules engine, integration with Companies House API, integration with GOV.UK Pay, and a notification service using GOV.UK Notify. The service runs on AWS ECS with an Aurora PostgreSQL database. The team has been focused on features and has minimal observability beyond basic CloudWatch metrics. The beta assessment is in 8 weeks, and assessors will ask about operational readiness.
workedExample.approach:
The Solution Architect designs an observability architecture that meets Service Standard requirements while being proportionate to the service's scale and team size.

Step 1 — Define SLOs based on user needs:
- Citizen SLO: 99.5% of application submissions complete successfully within 5 seconds
- Caseworker SLO: 99.9% of case actions complete within 2 seconds during business hours
- Integration SLO: 99% of Companies House lookups complete within 3 seconds (constrained by external dependency)
- Payment SLO: 99.9% of payment initiations succeed (failures mean citizens do not receive grants)

Step 2 — Implement correlation IDs:
- API gateway generates a UUID for every incoming request, set as X-Correlation-ID header
- All downstream services propagate this header in inter-service calls
- Message queues include the correlation ID in message attributes
- Every log entry includes the correlation_id field
- AWS X-Ray trace ID is linked to the correlation ID for end-to-end tracing

Step 3 — Structured logging standard:
- JSON format with fields: timestamp, correlation_id, service_name, service_version, level, message, and context-specific fields
- PII redaction: applicant names, addresses, and bank details are never logged; application reference numbers are used instead
- Logs shipped to CloudWatch Logs with a 90-day retention (meeting GovAssure requirements)
- Log insights queries pre-built for common diagnostic scenarios

Step 4 — Metric instrumentation:
- RED metrics (Rate, Errors, Duration) for every service endpoint
- Business metrics: applications submitted per hour, assessments completed per day, payments processed
- Dependency health: Companies House API response time and error rate, GOV.UK Pay response time
- Resource metrics: ECS CPU/memory, Aurora connections, queue depths

Step 5 — Alerting with runbooks:
- Alert: error budget burn rate exceeds 10x normal for citizen submission SLO → Runbook: check application service health, verify database connectivity, check for deployment correlation
- Alert: Companies House integration error rate exceeds 20% for 5 minutes → Runbook: verify Companies House API status page, check if specific query patterns are failing, consider enabling cached responses
- Alert: payment initiation failures exceed 1% → Runbook: check GOV.UK Pay status, verify API credentials have not expired, check if specific payment amounts are failing

Step 6 — Dashboards for audiences:
- Operations dashboard: real-time golden signals, dependency status, active alerts
- Service owner dashboard: SLO compliance over 30 days, error budget remaining, reliability trends
- Programme board view: RAG status for each SLO, key risks, next actions
workedExample.outcome: The service passes beta assessment with strong marks for operational readiness. Assessors specifically praise the clear SLOs linked to user needs, the correlation ID implementation enabling end-to-end request tracing, and the differentiated dashboards showing the team understands their different stakeholders. In the first month of beta, an intermittent database connection issue is identified through metric trends (connection pool saturation at specific times) before any user-visible failures occur — the team fixes it proactively. The Operations team transitions from reactive firefighting to proactive reliability management.
workedExample.lessonsLearned: Observability designed early is dramatically cheaper than observability retrofitted late. The 3 weeks spent on observability architecture saved many more weeks of incident investigation. The SLO-based approach prevented alert fatigue — the team receives 2-3 alerts per week, each meaningful and actionable, rather than dozens of noise alerts that trained them to ignore notifications. The correlation ID decision, made in sprint 2, proved invaluable for every subsequent debugging session.

civilServiceScenario.title: The Service That Failed Silently for Three Days
civilServiceScenario.background: A government department runs a citizen notification service that sends emails and letters about benefit changes. The service has been live for two years. It has basic logging (application logs written to files on the server) and a simple uptime monitor (pings the homepage every 5 minutes). There are no structured logs, no distributed tracing, no metrics beyond 'is the homepage responding', and no alerting on business outcomes. Last week, a database migration introduced a subtle bug: notifications were being marked as 'sent' in the database but the actual email/letter dispatch was silently failing. The homepage remained healthy. The uptime monitor showed 100%. For three days, 12,000 citizens did not receive notifications about benefit changes they needed to act on. The issue was discovered when citizens called the helpline to ask why they had not received expected letters.
civilServiceScenario.challenge: Design an observability architecture that would have detected this failure within minutes rather than days, and prevent similar silent failures in future.
constraints: The team has 4 developers and no dedicated SRE or platform engineer
Budget is limited — the solution must use existing AWS services rather than expensive third-party tooling
The service processes 5,000 notifications per day across email and letter channels
Letters are dispatched via a third-party print-and-post provider with a batch API
Emails are sent via GOV.UK Notify
The failure was silent because the dispatch function caught and swallowed exceptions after the migration
The team needs to demonstrate improved operational maturity for their next service assessment
GovAssure assessment is due in 4 months
civilServiceScenario.yourRole: You are the Solution Architect designing the observability improvement.
civilServiceScenario.discussion:
This scenario illustrates the danger of monitoring infrastructure health (is the server up?) without monitoring business outcomes (are notifications actually being delivered?). The homepage responding tells you nothing about whether the service is fulfilling its purpose.

The key observability gaps:
1. No business outcome metrics — nobody measured 'notifications successfully delivered per hour' against 'notifications queued per hour'. A simple comparison would have revealed the gap within minutes.
2. Exception swallowing — the code caught exceptions without logging them or raising alerts. Structured logging with mandatory error reporting would have surfaced this immediately.
3. No end-to-end validation — nobody checked whether GOV.UK Notify and the print provider were confirming receipt of dispatched items.
4. No correlation between intent and outcome — the system recorded 'marked as sent' but nobody verified 'actually received by delivery channel.'

The fix combines technical observability (structured logs, metrics on dispatch success/failure, alerts on delivery rate drops) with business observability (reconciliation between items queued, items dispatched, and delivery confirmations received). For a team of 4 without SRE expertise, CloudWatch Metrics with simple threshold alarms on business KPIs would have caught this in under 15 minutes.

practiceArtefact.description: Design an observability architecture for a government service that processes Freedom of Information (FOI) requests. The service receives 200 requests per day, involves caseworker assignment and workflow, integrates with a document management system, and must respond within 20 working days (statutory deadline). Define SLOs, describe your logging and metrics strategy, design alerting rules with runbooks, and explain how different stakeholders will access observability data.
practiceArtefact.guidance: Consider what 'silent failure' looks like for this service — it is not just the application crashing, but FOI requests stuck in workflow without progressing toward the 20-day deadline. Business metrics (requests approaching deadline without response, average time-in-stage) are as important as technical metrics. Think about what the Information Commissioner would want to see if they audited your response times.
practiceArtefact.modelAnswer:
**Observability Architecture: FOI Request Management Service**

**Service Level Objectives:**
- Availability SLO: 99.5% of requests to the service succeed during business hours (Mon-Fri 8am-6pm)
- Latency SLO: 99% of page loads complete within 3 seconds for caseworkers
- Business SLO: 95% of FOI requests receive a response within 15 working days (5-day buffer before the 20-day statutory limit)
- Integration SLO: 99% of document management system operations complete within 5 seconds

**Structured Logging Standard:**
- Format: JSON with fields — timestamp, correlation_id, service_name, level, message, foi_reference (never log request content or personal details of requesters)
- Retention: 2 years (aligned with ICO audit requirements)
- Key events logged: request received, caseworker assigned, each workflow stage transition, response dispatched, deadline approaching, deadline breached

**Metrics:**
- Technical: RED metrics on all endpoints, database connection pool utilisation, document management system response time
- Business: requests received per day, requests in each workflow stage, average days-in-stage, requests within 5 days of deadline, requests past deadline, caseworker workload distribution

**Alerting (with runbooks):**
- CRITICAL: Any request within 2 working days of deadline without a drafted response → Runbook: escalate to FOI team lead, check for blocked workflow, verify caseworker availability
- WARNING: Average time-in-stage exceeds 3 working days for any stage → Runbook: review stage for bottleneck, check caseworker capacity, consider process improvement
- WARNING: Document management system error rate exceeds 5% → Runbook: check DMS health, verify credentials, check storage capacity
- INFO: Daily digest of requests approaching deadline (sent every morning at 8am to FOI team lead)

**Dashboards:**
- Caseworker dashboard: my assigned requests, days remaining on each, blocked items
- Team lead dashboard: all requests by stage, approaching deadlines, caseworker workload balance
- Senior leadership: compliance rate (% responded within 20 days), trend over 12 months, comparison to ICO benchmarks
- Operations: service health, error rates, dependency status

reflectiveQuestions: Think about the last incident you were involved in. How long did it take to identify the root cause, and how much of that time was spent searching for relevant data? Would better observability have shortened this?

Does your current service have SLOs defined from the user's perspective, or only infrastructure metrics? Could you explain your service's reliability to a non-technical stakeholder using your current dashboards?
How would your team detect a 'silent failure' — where the service appears healthy but is not delivering its intended outcomes? What business-level metrics would reveal this?
Are your current alerts actionable? When your team receives an alert at 3am, do they know exactly what to check and what to do, or does it trigger a lengthy investigation?
If the GovAssure assessors asked you to demonstrate your incident detection and response capability tomorrow, what would you show them? What gaps would be embarrassing?

knowledgeCheck.question: What are the three pillars of observability?
options: Availability, performance, and security
Logs, metrics, and traces
Monitoring, alerting, and dashboards
CPU, memory, and network
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The three pillars of observability are logs (discrete event records), metrics (numerical measurements over time), and traces (request journeys across distributed services). Together they provide complementary views: metrics reveal problems exist, traces locate where they occur, and logs explain why.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the primary purpose of a correlation ID?
options: To encrypt data in transit between services
To trace a single request across multiple services for debugging and diagnosis
To authenticate users across different service boundaries
To load balance requests across multiple service instances
knowledgeCheck.explanation: A correlation ID is a unique identifier assigned to a request at its entry point and propagated through every service it touches. This enables engineers to search for one ID and see the complete journey of a request, making diagnosis of distributed system issues practical rather than guesswork.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why is SLO-based alerting preferred over threshold-based alerting?
options: SLOs are cheaper to implement than threshold alerts
SLO-based alerting fires when user experience is genuinely at risk, reducing noise and alert fatigue
Threshold alerts are not supported by modern monitoring tools
SLOs eliminate the need for on-call engineers entirely
knowledgeCheck.explanation: SLO-based alerting uses error budgets to determine when service reliability is genuinely at risk, only alerting when the burn rate threatens the committed service level. This reduces alert fatigue by eliminating alerts for brief spikes that self-resolve while still catching genuine problems that affect users.

knowledgeCheck.question: What requirement does the Service Standard place on operational monitoring?
options: Services must use specific commercial monitoring tools approved by GDS
Services must demonstrate they can monitor, detect problems, and respond to incidents effectively
Services only need uptime monitoring that pings the homepage
Monitoring is optional for internal-facing government services
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Service Standard point 14 requires services to operate reliably, which means demonstrating effective monitoring, incident detection, and response capabilities. At beta and live assessments, teams must show how they monitor production, detect problems, and learn from incidents. A basic homepage ping is insufficient.

knowledgeCheck.question: In the scenario where notifications were marked as 'sent' but never actually dispatched, what type of observability would have caught this earliest?
options: Infrastructure monitoring showing server CPU usage
Business outcome metrics comparing notifications queued against delivery confirmations received
Application logs showing successful database writes
Uptime monitoring confirming the homepage responds
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Business outcome metrics would reveal the gap between intent and outcome — notifications entering the queue vs confirmations from the delivery channel. Infrastructure monitoring, uptime checks, and database write logs would all appear healthy because the infrastructure was functioning; it was the business outcome (actual delivery) that failed silently.
